title: Since I held your feet
hook: since I grasped Your feet I look to no one else (Chaupai, savaiya)

segments.voice: Yesterday, knower of every heart, and your line, he knows the pain. Did you wonder, once, about someone's ache underneath? Today Chaupai's verse changes shape, near its end. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

A busy market. A big family wedding. A toddler in the middle of it, holding on to a parent's leg, and fine as long as they're holding on. They'll peer out at the noise and the strangers, even smile. The second they let go and lose sight of that leg, the whole world becomes terrifying. It's not that the crowd changed. What changed was whether they were holding on. Near the end of Chaupai, the meter shifts into a savaiya, a longer, rolling line, and the poet describes exactly that kind of holding on. Today: since I held your feet.
screen: `A TODDLER HOLDING A PARENT'S LEG.` → `LET GO, AND THE CROWD IS TERRIFYING.` → `WHAT CHANGED WAS THE HOLDING ON.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the verse begins: since I grasped your feet, I have not brought anyone else under my eye. Feet again. You met them near the start of the prayer, where the mind rests at the Lord's feet. Here the poet doesn't just rest there. He has grabbed hold. In South Asian custom, touching or holding someone's feet is what you do before a person you deeply honor: a grandparent, a teacher. To grasp them and not let go is the gesture of someone who has decided where they belong. Then the verse goes on. In paraphrase: Ram and Rahim, the Puranas and the Qur'an speak of many views, and I have not taken one as my own; the Smritis, Shastras and Vedas tell of many mysteries, and I know none of them; by your grace, O sword-bearer, I have not said this, it is all your own telling. Two things are worth hearing carefully here. First, readers take this in more than one way. Sikh teachers often hear it as single-pointed trust rather than a ruling on other scriptures, and point out that the Guru Granth Sahib itself holds the words of Hindu and Muslim saints. On that reading, it's about where the poet's own eyes rest. When you're holding on to the feet, you stop shopping among opinions. Second, look at the last line: I have not said this; it's all you. The Tenth Guru, poet, leader, founder of the Khalsa, signs the verse by saying it isn't his. That's the posture of someone holding on to feet. And one good word for it is trust. Not a list of things believed. A grip. Since I held your feet, the crowd has stopped being frightening.
screen: `SINCE I GRASPED YOUR FEET.` · `HOLDING FEET: DEEP HONOR.` · `WHERE HIS OWN EYES REST.` · `I HAVE NOT SAID THIS; IT'S ALL YOU.` · then, large: `HELD AT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing to trust. Sit and breathe slowly. Notice how many things you're half-holding right now: plans, worries, opinions, backup plans for the backup plans. You don't have to drop them all. Just choose one thing to trust today, fully, the way a child holds a leg in a crowd. It might be God, if you pray. It might be a person who has never let you down, or the fact that you've come through hard days before. Hold it in your mind, firmly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do. The bell holds the time.
Since I held your feet. Chaupai's savaiya: since I grasped your feet, I look to no one else, and what I've said was never mine.
screen: `SINCE I HELD YOUR FEET — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: held at the feet. Today, when the crowd of worries gets loud, picture your hand closing around the one thing you chose to trust. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya as part of Chaupai Sahib, and it is also included in the evening Rehras; touching the feet of elders and teachers is a common sign of deep respect in Punjabi culture.

original.note: Gurmukhi: charan, feet; in Chaupai, the place where the mind rests and the hands hold on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse saying other religions are wrong.
what it means: since I grasped your feet, I stopped looking elsewhere. read by Sikh teachers as single-pointed trust.
what a scholar hears: the verse ends 'main na kahio sabh tohi bakhaanio', I have not said it, you told it all, a signature of humility from the author of the Khalsa.
